title: How to use this manual
lead:
Read this page once. It is short, and it decides whether the rest of the
  manual works for you.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
This manual assumes you have never designed a database, never drawn an entity-relationship diagram, and never written a line of SQL. It carries you from there to a full mark in the examination. It is also meant to be enough on its own: you should never need a lecturer, a textbook or a website to follow it. Anything it uses, it teaches first, including its own notation.

In exchange it asks one thing: draw the diagrams and write the queries yourself. Reading a finished ER diagram or a solved normalization creates a feeling of understanding that evaporates in the examination hall, where you face a blank page and a business description. Every diagram in this book was drawn by hand first, and every query was checked against the schema it runs on. Do the same, and the difference between your answer and the one printed here is information.
Every page is built from a small set of boxes. Each has one job, and the colour tells you which before you read a word.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html: New ideas, explained from nothing. Read these properly.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html: Emerald green means learn this by heart. Definitions the examiner asks for word for word, the normal-form rules, the crow's-foot symbols, the six relational algebra operations. It is the only thing this colour is ever used for. If a page has green on it, there is something on that page you are expected to know cold.

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.tag: Solved right where it is taught
blocks.working:
A real question, solved in numbered steps, then a now you try at the end. Every worked box carries a small chip saying where the question comes from, so you know it is a question that was actually asked, not one invented to be easy:

PQ 25/26 Q6 a past paper (session and question); TEST 1 the class test; DECK the practice slides; TEXT M4U1 the course text's own exercise. Do the "now you try" before moving on.

blocks.label: SQL / Relational algebra
blocks.html: Indigo means a listing you would write on the answer sheet: an SQL statement or a relational algebra expression. It is always in a fixed-width font so the structure is exact. You are expected to be able to reproduce these, not just read them.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: A mistake that is easy to make and costly in marks. Most are taken from the exact places the examiner sets a snare: a partial dependency mistaken for transitive, a NULL that breaks a count, a many-to-many relationship with an attribute stranded on the line.

blocks.label: Recall
blocks.question: Questions with the answers printed underneath, below a dashed line. Cover the answers. Say your answer out loud, or write it, and only then look. Checking whether you knew something is not the same as knowing it, and the difference is the whole point of this box.

blocks.label: Exam question
blocks.printed:
A question reproduced as it appeared on the paper, plain and
    uncoloured, so you meet it the way the examiner set it. Its worked answer follows in a
    teal Answer box.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html: Half of this course is drawn, not written. An entity is a rectangle, a relationship a line with a verb on it, and the small marks at the ends of that line, the crow's foot, a circle, a single bar, carry the whole meaning of a business rule. Get a symbol wrong and the answer is wrong, however good the prose around it. Every symbol used in this manual is defined the first time it appears, and the full legend sits in Module Two. Where a figure is a diagram you must be able to draw, redraw it yourself until it comes out without looking.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
The promise. Every number, every normalized set of relations, and every query result in this manual was worked out independently, not copied from a source. The course's own materials contain arithmetic and design slips (you will meet one, a table whose printed candidate keys do not match its data), so nothing here is trusted just because a source printed it. Where a source is wrong, this manual says so and shows the correct working.

The label. A few questions in the past papers come from an older, wider syllabus (this course was once taught under a different code with extra "high performance" topics). Where a question or a piece of content is outside the current syllabus, it carries a Not in syllabus label. It is still taught and still solved in full, so that if it reappears you lose no marks, but the label tells you it is not core, so you spend your revision time accordingly.

part: Part A: what a database is
title: Foundations of Data Management
lead:
Before a single table is drawn, three questions: what is data, what do we
  actually do with it, and what makes a system that holds it good rather than merely
  large.

blocks.html: By the end of this unit you can: tell data from information; describe how data is captured, represented, stored, and retrieved; explain the difference between privacy, integrity, and security; and judge a system by its scalability, efficiency, and effectiveness.

A single value, 08:00, or Glasgow, or 350, is data: a raw fact with no context. On its own it tells you nothing. The moment you put it in context, "the 08:00 inspection of property PG4 in Glasgow was priced at 350", it becomes information: data that has been organised so a person can act on it.
Everything in this course is machinery for turning the first thing into the second reliably, for many users at once, without the facts contradicting each other. That is what "data management" means.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html: Data is raw, unprocessed facts. Information is data processed and placed in a context that gives it meaning. Data is the input; information is the output you can make a decision with.

blocks.text: 1.2 The information lifecycle: capture, represent, store, retrieve

blocks.html: Data enters a system, is put into a form a computer can hold, is kept safely, and is fetched again on demand. Four stages, in order:

Capture is how data is collected from the real world: manual entry on a form, sensors and IoT devices, scanners and OCR, or an API pulling from another system. Representation is the form it is stored in: every value is given a data type that fixes what it may hold and how much space it takes.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: Data types you will use all year
blocks.html:
TypeHoldsExample value
INT (INTEGER)whole numbers350
VARCHAR(n)text up to n characters'Glasgow'
CHAR(n)fixed-length text'M231 JGR'
DATEa calendar date'2004-10-18'
DECIMAL(p,s)exact numbers with decimals80000.00

You will meet these again the moment you write your first CREATE TABLE in Module Five. Text values go in single quotes; numbers do not.

Storing data well means being able to find it again quickly, which is the job of an index, and retrieval is fetching it with a query. Indexing earns its own question on the paper, so it earns a worked answer here.

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. What is the purpose of indexing in a database, and how does it improve performance?

  1. Say what an index is. An index is a separate lookup structure that maps the values of a column to the locations of the rows that hold them, in the way the index at the back of a book maps a topic to its page numbers.
  2. Say what it replaces. Without an index, finding every row where city = 'Glasgow' means reading every row in the table, a full table scan. On a million-row table that is a million reads.
  3. Say how it helps. With an index on city, the system jumps straight to the matching entries (using a structure such as a B-tree or a hash index) and reads only those rows. Search, sorting, and joining all get faster.
  4. State the cost, because a complete answer names the trade-off. An index takes extra storage and must be updated on every insert, update, and delete, so indexing every column would slow writing down. You index the columns you search on.
blocks.redo: Now you try: in one sentence each, give one column in a STAFF(staffNo, fName, lName, branchNo) table you would index and one you would not, and why.

blocks.text: 1.3 Three things people confuse: privacy, integrity, security

blocks.html: These three words are used loosely in ordinary speech and precisely in this course. The examiner asks you to separate them, so separate them.

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. Explain the differences between data privacy, data integrity, and data security.

Data privacy concerns who is permitted to access which data. It is enforced with access control (role-based permissions), anonymisation of sensitive fields, and compliance with data-protection law. Example: an ordinary student may see their own results but not a lecturer's salary.

Data integrity concerns whether the data is accurate and consistent. It is enforced with constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK), referential integrity (foreign keys that must match a real row), and transaction management so a half-finished update never leaves the data in a broken state. Example: a booking cannot reference a guest number that does not exist.

Data security concerns protection against unauthorised access and attack. It is enforced with authentication, encryption, firewalls, database hardening, and backups for disaster recovery. Example: passwords are stored encrypted, not in plain text.

One-line hook to remember them: privacy = who may see it, integrity = is it correct, security = keeping attackers out.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html: Integrity leans on the transaction, and a good transaction has four properties, ACID: Atomicity (all of it happens or none of it does), Consistency (it moves the database from one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not tread on each other), Durability (once committed, it survives a crash). Learn the word and what each letter means.

blocks.text: 1.4 Judging a system: scalability, efficiency, effectiveness

blocks.html: Three attributes decide whether a data system is any good. They sound similar and are not.

• Scalability is the ability to keep working as data and users grow. You scale vertically by giving one machine more power (more CPU, memory, disk), or horizontally by spreading the load across many machines (replication, sharding).
  • Efficiency is how little resource the work costs: CPU, memory, storage, and query time. Good indexing and storage design buy efficiency.
  • Effectiveness is whether the system actually meets the users' needs: accurate results, reliable uptime, and user satisfaction.
The distinction between the last two is a favourite short question, so here it is, answered.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: 6 (a) Differentiate between Information Efficiency and Information Effectiveness    [3 Marks]

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. Differentiate between Information Efficiency and Information Effectiveness. Not in syllabus (phrased in the older wording; the ideas are the efficiency/effectiveness pair above, so you can still answer it fully.)

Information efficiency is about doing the thing right: producing the required information with the least resource and time, cost per query, storage used, response time. A report that is generated in one second using little memory is efficient.

Information effectiveness is about doing the right thing: producing information that actually serves the user's purpose, that is accurate, relevant, timely and complete enough to decide on. A report delivered instantly but showing the wrong figures is efficient yet not effective.

Hook: efficiency = doing it right (cheaply, quickly); effectiveness = doing the right thing (usefully, correctly).

blocks.label: Recall
blocks.question:
1. Give one sentence separating data from information.

2. Name the four stages of the information lifecycle in order.

3. Which of privacy, integrity, security does a foreign key serve?

4. What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?

Answers

1. Data is raw facts; information is data given context so it can be acted on. 2. Capture, represent, store, retrieve. 3. Integrity (it keeps references correct). 4. Vertical = one bigger machine; horizontal = more machines sharing the load.

part: Part A: what a database is
title: Database Systems and Architecture
lead:
Why organisations abandoned loose files for databases, what a DBMS is and
  what sits inside it, and the layered architecture that lets the data and the programs
  change independently.

blocks.html: By the end of this unit you can: list the limitations of the file-based approach and the advantages of the database approach; define a database, a DBMS, a schema, and an instance; separate DDL from DML; explain the three levels of data abstraction and the two kinds of data independence; and tell a personal database from an enterprise one.

blocks.text: 2.1 The file-based approach, and why it failed

blocks.html: Before databases, each part of an organisation kept its own files and wrote its own programs to read them. The sales department had a sales file; accounts had an accounts file; each with its own copy of the customer list. This is the file-based approach, and it fails in ways the examiner returns to every year.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
• Data redundancy. The same fact (a customer's address) is stored in several files.
  • Data inconsistency. Update it in one file and not another, and the copies now disagree.
  • Data isolation. Data is scattered across files in different formats, so writing a program to combine it is hard.
  • Program-data dependence. The file's structure is written into every program, so changing the structure means rewriting the programs.
  • Difficult concurrent access. Letting many users write at once safely is left to each program to solve, and mostly it is not solved.
  • Weak security and integrity. Rules live in program code, applied unevenly, easy to bypass.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: a. Explain two (2) limitations of the file-based approach to data processing.   (2 mks)

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.tag: PQ 25/26 Q2a · also PQ 20/21 Q1a , PQ 15/16 Q1c
blocks.working:
Q. Explain two limitations of the file-based approach to data processing. (25/26 asks for two; 20/21 asks for three; 15/16 asks for five. One answer, scaled to the marks.)

Model answer (two, stated then explained)

1. Data redundancy and inconsistency. Because each program keeps its own files, the same data is duplicated across them. When one copy is updated and another is not, the files disagree, and there is no single correct version.

2. Program-data dependence. The physical structure of a file (its fields and their order) is embedded in the code of every program that reads it. A change as small as widening a field forces a change to every one of those programs.

For three, add data isolation (data scattered in incompatible formats is hard to combine). For five, add difficulty of concurrent access and weak security and integrity control. Naming the limitation and then explaining it in a sentence is what earns the mark; a bare list does not.
blocks.redo: Now you try: the database approach fixes each of these. For redundancy and for program-data dependence, name the database feature that removes it. (Answers appear in 2.4 and 2.5 below.)

blocks.html: Four definitions the examiner asks for by name. Learn them in these words.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
Database: a shared collection of logically related data (and a description of that data), designed to meet the information needs of an organisation.

DBMS (Database Management System): the software that lets users define, create, maintain, and control access to the database. Examples: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server.

Schema: the description of the data using a given data model, that is, the structure. It changes rarely. Example: Student{matricNo, name, address, programme, age}.

Instance (database instance): the actual data in the database at a particular moment. It changes constantly, on every insert, update, and delete.

Schema is to instance as the empty form is to the filled-in form: the form's layout is the schema, today's stack of completed forms is the instance.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: (c)  With two (2) examples, describe a database management system                (3½ marks)

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. With two examples, describe a Database Management System. (24/25 Q4c) And define: data model, database instance, DBMS. (19/20 Q2c)

A DBMS is the software layer between the users and the stored data. It lets them define the structure (through a data-definition language), put data in and take it out (through a data-manipulation language), and it controls access, enforces integrity, and manages concurrency and recovery, so the applications do not each have to. Two examples: MySQL and Oracle Database (also acceptable: PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, IBM Db2).

A data model is a collection of concepts used to describe the structure of a database, that is, the data, the relationships between it, and the constraints on it. The relational model (tables) is the one this course centres on.

A database instance is the information held in the database at a particular point in time, a snapshot of its current contents.

blocks.text: 2.3 Two languages inside the DBMS: DDL and DML

blocks.html: You talk to a database in two registers. One defines the structure; the other moves the data around.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
DDL (Data Definition Language)DML (Data Manipulation Language)
Definesthe structure: entities, attributes, relationships, constraintsthe data: the rows themselves
Acts onthe schemathe instance
StatementsCREATE, ALTER, DROPINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT
Compiles intotables stored in the data dictionary (system catalogue: metadata, "data about data")changes to the stored rows

The retrieval-only part of DML (the SELECT) is called a query language. The four DML operations are retrieval, insertion, deletion, and modification.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(d)  Differentiate between data definition language (DDL) and data manipulation language (DML)
                                                                     (3 marks)


Question Five

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. Differentiate between data definition language (DDL) and data manipulation language (DML).

DDL is the part of a database language used to define and change the structure of the database: creating tables, altering columns, dropping objects, and stating constraints. Its statements are CREATE, ALTER, and DROP, and their effect is recorded in the data dictionary.

DML is the part used to work with the data itself: inserting new rows, updating and deleting existing ones, and retrieving them. Its statements are INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and SELECT.

In short: DDL changes the container, DML changes the contents.

blocks.text: 2.4 Inside the DBMS: its components and its people

blocks.html: A DBMS is not one program but several parts working together, and it is run by people with defined roles. Two roles are regularly confused on the paper.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html: Asked to "list components of a DBMS", name from this set: the DDL compiler, the DML compiler / query language processor, the query processor (breaks a request into steps), the database manager (moves data between disk and memory), the file manager, the data dictionary / system catalogue, the DML pre-compiler, the authorisation and integrity manager, the transaction manager, and the recovery / backup manager. The database manager is the module that interfaces between the low-level stored data and the application programs and queries.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: 4 (b) Explain Database Manager and its Responsibilities                      [3.5 Marks]

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. Explain the Database Manager and its responsibilities, and differentiate it from the Database Administrator.

The Database Manager is a software module inside the DBMS. It is the interface between the low-level data stored on disk and the application programs and queries that ask for it. Its responsibilities are moving data between disk and main memory, and enforcing, at run time, the integrity and access controls the database is set up with. It is a program.

The Database Administrator (DBA) is a person with central control over the data and the programs that access it. Their responsibilities are: defining the schema, granting authorisation for data access, specifying integrity constraints, defining storage structures and access methods, and modifying the schema or physical organisation as needs change.

The one-line separation: the Database Manager is a program inside the DBMS; the Database Administrator is a person who runs the database.

blocks.text: 2.5 The layered architecture: three levels of data abstraction

blocks.html: This is the central idea of the whole unit, and the answer to the "program-data dependence" problem from 2.1. A database hides its physical storage behind layers, so that a user sees only what they need and a change at one layer does not ripple up to the next. The classic picture is the three-schema architecture, also called the three levels of data abstraction.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
External level (view level): the highest. Each user or program sees only the slice of data relevant to it, as rows and columns, tailored to its access rights. A student's view can compute a CGPA or an age without ever seeing a lecturer's salary. Many different external views can exist over the same data.

Conceptual level (logical level): the middle. It describes all the data in the database as tables and the relationships between them, without any concern for how it is stored. This is the level the database designer works at.

Internal level (physical level): the lowest. It describes how the data is actually stored: the file organisation, the indexes, whether hashing or a B+ tree is used. (Some texts name a separate physical level below the internal one; the exam wants the three: external, conceptual, internal.)

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
c. What is meant by data abstraction? Explain the three (3) levels of data abstraction with
   examples.                                                 (5 ½ mks)

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. What is meant by data abstraction? Explain the three levels of data abstraction with examples. (25/26 Q2c) Equivalently: explain the differences between user views, a conceptual schema, and an internal schema as different perspectives of the same database. (19/20 Q1b)

Data abstraction is the hiding of the complex details of how data is stored, showing each user only what they need. It is what lets a user work with a table without knowing anything about disks or files.

  1. External level (user views). What one user or program sees: a customised subset of the data. Example: the "Student" view shows a student their courses and results but not other students' records, and not any salary data.
  2. Conceptual level (conceptual schema). The community view: every table and relationship in the database, described independently of storage. Example: the whole university schema, STUDENT, COURSE, LECTURER, DEPARTMENT, and how they relate.
  3. Internal level (internal schema). The storage view: how those tables are physically held, which files, which indexes, which access method. Example: STUDENT is stored as an indexed file with a B+ tree index on matricNo.

They are three perspectives on one database: the same STUDENT data, seen as a tailored view, as a logical table, and as bytes in an indexed file.

blocks.text: 2.6 Why the layers matter: data independence

blocks.html: The layers are not decoration. They deliver data independence: the ability to change the schema at one level without having to change the level above it. This is the precise cure for the file-based approach's program-data dependence.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
Physical data independence: the ability to change the internal (physical) schema, adding an index, changing the file organisation, without changing the conceptual schema or rewriting any application program. Comparatively easy to achieve.

Logical data independence: the ability to change the conceptual schema, adding a column or a table, without changing the external views or rewriting programs that do not use the change. Harder to achieve, because programs depend closely on the logical structure.

Example of logical independence: users A and B both read EmployeeNumber and EmployeeName. B adds a Salary column to the schema. A's view and A's programs are untouched.

blocks.text: 2.7 Two sizes of database: personal and enterprise

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html: A personal database system supports a single application with a few tables, on one computer, for one user: simple. An enterprise-level database system supports many users at once and multiple applications, across many computers, with many tables and often many databases: complex. The difference the examiner wants is number of users, number of applications, and complexity.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
a. (i)    Would you choose a database system instead of simply storing data in operating
          system files? Justify your answer with two points.        (5 marks)
   (ii)   When would it make sense not to use a database system?    (2.5 marks)

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q(i). Would you choose a database system instead of simply storing data in operating-system files? Justify with two points. Q(ii). When would it make sense not to use a database system?

(i) Yes, choose a database, because:

1. Controlled, consistent, shared access. A DBMS gives one shared copy of the data with concurrency control, so many users can read and write at once without corrupting it or duplicating it, which loose OS files cannot do safely.

2. Integrity, security, and independence built in. Constraints and access control are enforced centrally, and the layered architecture gives data independence, so the structure can change without rewriting every program. With OS files, all of this is left to hand-written code.

(ii) When not to use one

A database system carries cost and overhead (licensing, hardware, expertise, and slower simple access). For a small, single-user, single-application task with little data, few or no concurrency needs, and a fixed structure, plain files are cheaper and simpler, and a full DBMS is not worth its overhead. Real-time systems with very tight timing, or purely temporary data, are other cases where files can be preferable.

blocks.label: Recall
blocks.question:
1. Two limitations of the file-based approach.

2. Which language creates a table, DDL or DML? Which inserts a row?

3. Name the three levels of data abstraction, highest first.

4. Which is harder to achieve, physical or logical data independence?

5. Database Manager or DBA: which one is a person?

Answers

1. Any two of: redundancy, inconsistency, isolation, program-data dependence, poor concurrency, weak security/integrity. 2. DDL creates the table (CREATE); DML inserts the row (INSERT). 3. External, conceptual, internal. 4. Logical. 5. The DBA is the person; the Database Manager is a software module.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html: You now have the vocabulary: data and information, DBMS, schema and instance, DDL and DML, the three levels, data independence. Module Two turns to the conceptual level and how you design it: the entity-relationship diagram, where a business description in English becomes a picture, and then, in Module Three, a set of tables. That picture is the single most drawn thing on the examination paper, so that is where we go next.

title: The Entity-Relationship Model
lead:
A business hands you a description in words. Your job is to draw it: the
  things it cares about, how they connect, and the rules governing those connections. That
  drawing is the entity-relationship diagram, and drawing it correctly is half of this
  course's marks.

blocks.html: By the end of this unit you can: extract business rules from a description; draw entities, attributes, and relationships in a consistent notation; read and set cardinality with the crow's-foot symbols; and turn any of the recurring exam scenarios into a correct ER diagram.

blocks.text: 1.1 From words to a model: business rules

blocks.html: A conceptual model is a high-level picture of the data an organisation cares about and how it relates, drawn without any concern for how a computer will store it. The entity-relationship (E-R) model is the most widely used one, and an ER diagram (ERD) is its picture. It is independent of any particular DBMS.

Everything in the diagram comes from business rules: statements, drawn from the organisation's policies and procedures, about the structure and behaviour of its data. A business rule is also called an integrity constraint once it is in the database. A rule such as "each project is contracted by exactly one client" is what fixes a cardinality on your diagram.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: Characteristics of a good business rule
blocks.html:
A good business rule is:

  • Declarative: it states what should be true, not how to enforce it.
  • Precise: it has one clear, unambiguous meaning.
  • Atomic: it states one single thing, not several.
  • Consistent: it does not contradict another rule.
  • Expressible: it can be written in plain language.
  • Distinct: it does not duplicate another rule.
  • Business-oriented: it is stated in terms the business understands.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(b) Business rule is important in data modelling, as it represent an organisation operation interaction
    among the stakeholders and the data flow. As a database administrator you have been asked by the
    management of Alex & Suite legal firm to come up with a standard business rule that will capture
    their organisation operation interaction and data flow. Explain Four important qualities you will
    need to consider in making your delivery.                        (4marks)

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. State four qualities you would consider in making a good business rule (21/22 asks for four characteristics of a good business rule).

Any four of the seven above, each named and given a phrase: a good business rule is declarative (states what is true, not how to enforce it), precise (one unambiguous meaning), atomic (states a single fact), and business-oriented (expressed in the organisation's own terms). Naming and explaining four earns full marks; a bare list of words does not.

blocks.text: 1.2 The notation, all of it, on one page

blocks.html: There is no single world standard for ER notation. This manual uses the common crow's-foot style that the recent papers use. Learn these symbols cold: an answer with the right idea and the wrong symbol is still marked wrong.

An entity is a person, place, object, event, or concept the organisation keeps data about. It is named with a noun, in capitals, singular: EMPLOYEE, PROPERTY, SALE. Two distinctions the examiner tests by name:

• Entity type vs entity instance. The entity type is the general category, EMPLOYEE, described once. An instance is one particular occurrence, the employee "S011, Tony Smith".
  • Strong vs weak entity. A strong (independent) entity exists on its own and has its own identifier. A weak (dependent) entity cannot exist without another entity, its identifying owner, and has no full identifier of its own, only a partial identifier. It is drawn with a double border.

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. Explain, with an example: weak entity type, strong entity type, unary relationship.

Weak entity type: an entity type whose existence depends on another entity type; a dependent entity that has no business meaning in the diagram without its owner. Example: a DEPENDENT of an employee (it exists only while the EMPLOYEE does).

Strong entity type: an entity type that exists independently of any other; an independent entity with its own identifier. Example: EMPLOYEE.

Unary relationship: a relationship between the instances of a single entity type; also called a recursive relationship. Example: an EMPLOYEE "manages" another EMPLOYEE. (Diagram in section 1.5.)

blocks.html: An attribute is a property of an entity, named with a noun. The types you must distinguish, because the examiner asks you to:

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
• Simple: cannot be broken down (age).
  • Composite: made of parts (Name = firstName + lastName; Address = street + city + postcode).
  • Multivalued: may hold more than one value per instance (an employee's {skills}). Shown in curly braces.
  • Derived: calculated from other data ([age] from date of birth). Shown in square brackets.
  • Identifier (key): distinguishes instances; no two share it. Shown underlined. A composite identifier is made of more than one attribute.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(a)  Differentiate between the following relational concepts with an example
     (i)     Associative entity and ternary relationship.            (2½marks)
     (ii)    Multivalued attributes and derived attributes.          (2½marks)

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. Differentiate, with an example: (i) multivalued vs derived attribute; (ii) composite vs multivalued attribute.

A multivalued attribute can take several values at once for one instance, for example an employee's {skills} = {Java, SQL, French}. A derived attribute holds a value worked out from other stored data, not stored in its own right, for example [age] computed from dateOfBirth and today's date. One holds many real values; the other holds a computed one.

A composite attribute is one attribute divided into sub-parts, for example Address into (street, city, postcode). A multivalued attribute is one attribute with several values of the same kind, for example {phoneNumbers}. Composite is one value in parts; multivalued is several values.

title: The Enhanced E-R Model
lead:
When some things are special kinds of other things, an employee who is
  either hourly or salaried, an offering that is either a product or a service, the plain ER
  model is not enough. The enhanced ER model adds one construct, the supertype and its
  subtypes, and four rules that go with it. Those rules are examined every single year.

blocks.html: By the end of this unit you can: tell a supertype from a subtype; distinguish generalization from specialization; apply the completeness (total/partial) and disjointness (disjoint/overlap) constraints; use a subtype discriminator; and draw any supertype/subtype hierarchy the paper asks for.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html: A subtype is a meaningful subgrouping of the entities in an entity type, for example GRADUATE and UNDERGRADUATE within STUDENT. A supertype is the generic entity type that holds what the subgroups have in common, for example STUDENT. The relationship is drawn with a circle between the supertype and its subtypes, and the subtypes connect to it with the subset symbol.

You use a supertype/subtype structure when either (a) some attributes apply only to some instances (only salaried employees have an annual salary), or (b) some instances take part in a relationship that others do not (only consultants relate to a CONTRACT).

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html: A subtype inherits every attribute and every relationship of its supertype. Attributes are placed at the highest level to which they apply: SSN at PERSON, dateHired at EMPLOYEE, rank at FACULTY. So a FACULTY instance has SSN, Name (from PERSON), dateHired, salary (from EMPLOYEE), and rank (from FACULTY). This is why the structure avoids redundancy: the common attributes are stored once, at the top.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(a)  Briefly differentiate the following pair of concepts with example
     (i)   Total specialization and partial specialization.          (2½marks)
     (ii)  Supertype and subtype.                                    (2½marks)

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. Differentiate: (i) supertype and subtype; (ii) generalization and specialization.

Supertype vs subtype: a supertype is the general entity type holding common attributes; a subtype is a specialised subgroup of it holding its own extra attributes and inheriting the supertype's. VEHICLE is a supertype; CAR and TRUCK are subtypes.

Generalization vs specialization: both build the same hierarchy but from opposite ends. Generalization is bottom-up: you start with specialised entity types (CAR, TRUCK) and define a general supertype (VEHICLE) from what they share. Specialization is top-down: you start with a general entity type (VEHICLE) and define subtypes (CAR, TRUCK) for the parts that differ.

blocks.text: 2.3 The two constraints you are always asked for

blocks.html: Every EER question turns on two independent choices. Get them both and you have the diagram.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
Completeness (does every supertype instance have to be a subtype?)

  • Total specialization: yes, every supertype instance must belong to some subtype. Drawn with a double line from the supertype to the circle.
  • Partial specialization: no, a supertype instance need not belong to any subtype. Drawn with a single line.

Disjointness (can an instance be more than one subtype at once?)

  • Disjoint rule (d): no, an instance is at most one subtype. Circle marked d.
  • Overlap rule (o): yes, an instance may be several subtypes at once. Circle marked o.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html: One more mark the paper asks for by name. The subtype discriminator (also called the discriminating attribute) is a supertype attribute whose value says which subtype a row belongs to. It is written beside the specialization circle. For a disjoint specialization it holds one value per row (for EMPLOYEE over SALARIED and HOURLY, a discriminator empType reads "S" or "H"). For an overlap specialization one value is not enough, so the discriminator is a set of yes/no flags, one per subtype.

blocks.printed:

    (ii)    Required attribute                                       (1½ marks)
    (iii)   Disjoint rule                                            (1½ marks)
    (iv)    Overlap rule                                             (1½ marks)

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. Explain: total vs partial specialization; disjoint rule vs overlap rule; entity type; required attribute.

Total specialization: every instance of the supertype must be a member of at least one subtype. Partial specialization: a supertype instance need not be a member of any subtype. Disjoint rule: a supertype instance that is in one subtype cannot at the same time be in another. Overlap rule: a supertype instance may be a member of two or more subtypes at the same time. Entity type: a collection of entities sharing common properties, described once (EMPLOYEE). Required attribute: an attribute that must have a value for every instance (an employee's empID).

title: Semi-Structured Models: XML and JSON
lead:
Not all data fits neatly into a table with fixed columns. Semi-structured
  models keep some structure, tags and nesting, while letting every record differ. XML and
  JSON are the two you must be able to read and write.

blocks.html: By the end of this unit you can: say what semi-structured data is and when it is used; read and write both XML and JSON; and explain how XML data is stored, queried, and displayed.

A structured model (the relational table) has a fixed schema: every row has the same columns. Unstructured data (a plain document, an image) has none. A semi-structured model sits between: it carries structure through tags or keys, but the structure can vary from one record to the next and change often.

• Flexible schema. Two forms: wide-column, where the set of attributes is not fixed and new ones are added as needed; and sparse-column, where there is a fixed but huge set of possible attributes and each record fills in only the few it uses, the rest left null.
  • Multivalued types. An attribute may hold a set or array of values, for example interests = {basketball, cooking, jazz}, which a flat table forbids.
  • Nested types. An attribute may itself be structured, for example name broken into first and last. The two models built on these ideas are JSON and XML.

blocks.text: 3.2 JSON and XML, side by side

blocks.html: Both represent the same fact. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) uses braces and key-value pairs; XML (eXtensible Markup Language) uses paired tags in angle brackets. The same staff record in each:

Both are self-describing (the tags or keys name the data), hierarchical (values nest inside values), and need no fixed schema. XML tags always come in pairs, <tag>...</tag>, and can represent both relational rows and tree-shaped documents such as a purchase order with nested line items.

• Storing. Three ways: shredding it into relational tables (each element to a column, with relationship tables); a dedicated XML column type (optionally validated against an XSD schema); or a purpose-built native XML database.
  • Querying. XPath expressions locate data by a path through the tree; XQuery is the full query language built on XPath. As the text puts it, "XQuery is to XML as SQL is to relational databases".
  • Displaying. A stylesheet in XSL (Extensible Stylesheet Language), applied through XSLT, transforms XML into a display format such as an HTML table, so the same data can render on a phone, a tablet, or a page.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
• Schema flexibility: no fixed schema; fields vary per record.
  • Hierarchical structure: data nests in trees or graphs.
  • Self-describing: tags or keys carry the data's own metadata.
  • Partial organisation: more manageable than unstructured data because the tags impose some order.

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Is XML the same as HTML? Justify. No. HTML has a fixed set of tags with a fixed meaning, and its job is to display content in a browser. XML lets you define your own tags, and its job is to describe and carry data, not to display it. HTML says how something looks; XML says what something is.

Explain the semi-structured data types. Flexible-schema records (wide-column and sparse-column), multivalued attributes (sets or arrays of values), and nested attributes (structured values within values), as realised by JSON and XML.

Four inconveniences of semi-structured models (TMA): no enforced schema so data quality is harder to guarantee; querying is less mature than SQL (XQuery is not widely adopted); larger storage because tags repeat on every record; and weaker support for the integrity constraints a relational DBMS enforces automatically.

Q. Differentiate between SQL and NoSQL databases.

A SQL (relational) database stores data in tables with a fixed schema and relationships enforced by keys, and is queried with SQL; it favours strong consistency and structured data. A NoSQL database stores data in flexible forms (documents, key-value pairs, wide-columns, graphs) with little or no fixed schema, and scales out across many machines; it favours flexibility and horizontal scaling over strict structure. blocks.working:
Q. Describe the relational data model; and define relation, relational algebra, data model, attribute and tuple, domain, degree and cardinality.

The relational data model represents all data as a collection of relations (two-dimensional tables of rows and columns), where relationships between data are expressed by common values, not by pointers. A relation is a table with named columns and unordered rows. Relational algebra is the set of operations (select, project, join, and so on) used to query relations, covered in Module Five. A data model is a collection of concepts for describing data, its relationships, and its constraints. An attribute is a column; a tuple is a row. A domain is the set of permitted values of an attribute. Degree is the number of attributes; cardinality is the number of tuples.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
• Super key: any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple (may include extra, unnecessary attributes).
  • Candidate key: a minimal super key, one with no unnecessary attribute removed. A relation may have several.
  • Primary key (PK): the one candidate key chosen to identify tuples. Cannot be null.
  • Alternate key: a candidate key not chosen as the primary key.
  • Foreign key (FK): an attribute in one relation whose values must match the primary key of another (or be null); this is what links tables.

From here on, schema listings write PK for the primary key and FK for a foreign key, so a relation such as ROOM(roomNo, hotelNo, price) is annotated PK roomNo, hotelNo · FK hotelNo -> HOTEL.

Q. What is the relationship between a candidate key and a foreign key?

A candidate key uniquely identifies tuples within its own relation. A foreign key refers from one relation to a candidate key (in practice the primary key) of another. So a foreign key's whole purpose is to point at a candidate key elsewhere: the candidate key is the target, the foreign key is the pointer, and referential integrity is the rule that the pointer must always find its target.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
Entity integrity: no part of a primary key may be null. (If it were, the row could not be identified.)

Referential integrity: every foreign-key value must either match an existing primary-key value in the referenced relation, or be wholly null. (No row may point at a row that does not exist.)

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
• Each strong entity becomes a relation; its identifier becomes the primary key.
  • A one-to-many relationship puts the primary key of the "one" side into the "many" side as a foreign key.
  • A many-to-many relationship becomes its own relation, whose primary key is the two entities' keys together, plus any relationship attributes.
  • A one-to-one relationship puts the key of one side into the other as a foreign key (usually on the optional side).

  • A weak entity becomes a relation whose primary key includes the identifying owner's key.
  • A supertype/subtype maps either to one relation with all attributes (plus a type flag), or to a relation per subtype sharing the supertype's key. The common choice: one relation for the supertype and one per subtype, each subtype keyed by the supertype's key.

title: Normalization
lead:
A procedure with a fixed set of steps. You are given a table and its
  functional dependencies; you produce a set of relations in third normal form, or Boyce-Codd
  normal form, showing your working. Master one worked example and the rest are the same
  moves.

blocks.html: By the end of this unit you can: define full, partial, and transitive functional dependencies; draw a functional-dependency diagram; and normalize any given table to 3NF or BCNF, stating every step and the resulting relations.

Put everything in one table and three faults appear. Insertion anomaly: you cannot record a new property until someone inspects it, because inspection data shares the row. Update anomaly: a staff member's name, repeated on every inspection row, must be changed in every one or the copies disagree. Deletion anomaly: deleting the last inspection of a property loses the property's address too. Normalization removes all three by giving each fact one home.
An attribute B is functionally dependent on A, written A → B, if each value of A has exactly one value of B. A is the determinant. Three kinds are examined by name:

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
• Full functional dependency: B depends on the whole of a composite determinant A, not on any part of it. (propertyNo, iDate) → iTime is full: you need both.
  • Partial functional dependency: B depends on only part of a composite key. With key (propertyNo, iDate), propertyNo → pAddress is partial: pAddress needs only propertyNo.
  • Transitive functional dependency: B depends on the key only through another non-key attribute. (propertyNo, iDate) → staffNo → sName makes sName transitively dependent.

Q. Explain full, partial, and transitive functional dependency with examples; and explain a determinant.

A determinant is the attribute (or set of attributes) on the left of a functional dependency, the thing that determines another. In fd propertyNo → pAddress, propertyNo is the determinant. The three dependency types are in the box above; the one-line hooks are: full needs the whole composite key, partial needs only part of it, transitive reaches the key only through a non-key attribute. (For 25/26's EMPLOYEE2, the determinants are EmpID → Name, DeptName, Salary, and the composite (EmpID, CourseTitle) → DateCompleted, the only full dependency.)

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
• 1NF (first normal form): every cell holds a single value; no repeating groups.
  • 2NF (second normal form): in 1NF, and no partial dependency (every non-key attribute depends on the whole key).
  • 3NF (third normal form): in 2NF, and no transitive dependency (no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute).
  • BCNF (Boyce-Codd normal form): in 3NF, and every determinant is a candidate key. The strictest of the four.

The pattern is always the same: 2NF removes partial dependencies, 3NF removes transitive dependencies, BCNF removes any determinant that is not a candidate key.

Candidate keys

To 2NF (remove partial dependency)

Appointment(PNo, ADate, StaffNo, ATime)
   PK (PNo, ADate)  FK PNo -> Patient  FK StaffNo -> Staff

Check each relation's determinants. Patient (PNo), Staff (StaffNo), SurgeonAssign (StaffNo, ADate) are each keyed by their determinant. In Appointment, both (PNo, ADate) and (StaffNo, ADate, ATime) are candidate keys, and they are the only determinants, so every determinant is a candidate key. QUESTION THREE

blocks.label: Worked
blocks.working:
Q. R has attributes ABCD with FDs C → D, C → A, B → C. Find the candidate key, the best normal form R is in, and decompose to BCNF.

Candidate key. B determines C (given), C determines A and D, so B determines A, C, D, hence B determines everything: B is the sole candidate key.

Best normal form. Non-key attributes are A, C, D. B → C → A and B → C → D are transitive dependencies, so R is not in 3NF. There is no partial dependency (the key B is a single attribute), so R is in 2NF but not 3NF.

Decompose to BCNF. The offending determinant is C (not a candidate key). Split it off:

R1(C, A, D)    PK C     (from C -> A, C -> D)
R2(B, C)       PK B     FK C -> R1     (from B -> C)

Now every determinant (C in R1, B in R2) is a candidate key of its relation, and the join of R1 and R2 on C reconstructs R, so the decomposition is lossless and dependency-preserving.

part: Part D: asking questions of it
title: Relational Algebra
lead:
A small set of operations that each take one or two relations and produce a
  new relation. Chain them and you can express any query. The exam asks you to define the
  operations and to write expressions, so this unit does both.

blocks.html: By the end of this unit you can: define the six core operations with their symbols, and write a relational-algebra expression for any query over a given schema.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
OperationSymbolDoes
Selectionσ (sigma)picks rows that meet a condition: σprice<40(Room)
Projectionπ (pi)picks columns: πname,city(Hotel)
Union∪all rows in either relation (same columns), duplicates removed
Set difference−rows in the first relation but not the second
Cartesian product×every row of one paired with every row of the other
Join⋈ (bowtie)a product kept only where a matching condition holds

Two more you will use: rename ρ (rho), which gives a relation or its columns a new name, and division ÷, which finds rows associated with all rows of another relation ("works on all projects").

The three basic ones the older paper wants are selection (σ, choose rows), projection (π, choose columns), and join (⋈, combine two relations on a match). part: Part D: asking questions of it
title: Structured Query Language (SQL)
lead:
The language you actually type. SQL both defines the tables (DDL) and works
  with the data in them (DML). The exam gives you a schema and a list of English requests;
  your job is to write the statement for each. Every keyword below is introduced before it is
  used.

blocks.html: By the end of this unit you can: create, alter, and drop tables with keys and constraints; insert, update, and delete rows; and write a SELECT for any request using WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, the aggregate functions, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN, joins, subqueries, and views.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
CREATE TABLE Branch (
  branchNo  CHAR(4)     PRIMARY KEY,
  city      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL );

ALTER TABLE Staff DROP COLUMN DOB;          -- remove a column
ALTER TABLE Staff ADD prefRooms INT;        -- add a column
DROP TABLE Branch;                          -- remove the whole table

PRIMARY KEY enforces entity integrity; FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES enforces referential integrity; NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, and CHECK are the other constraints.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
INSERT INTO Emp VALUES (101, 'Azi Esther', 40, 15000);
UPDATE  Emp SET Salary = Salary * 1.10;          -- every row: 10% rise
DELETE  FROM Dept WHERE Dname = 'Toy';           -- only matching rows

An UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE touches every row. Text values are quoted; numbers are not.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
SELECT   columns (or * for all, or COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX)
FROM     table(s)
WHERE    row condition   (=, <, >, AND, OR, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN, IS NULL)
GROUP BY column          (one result row per group)
HAVING   group condition
ORDER BY column [ASC|DESC];

LIKE '%London%' matches any text containing London; IN ('a','b') matches a list; BETWEEN 200 AND 300 is an inclusive range; COUNT(*) counts rows. A join combines tables on a matching column; a subquery is a SELECT inside another; a view is a stored SELECT (CREATE VIEW).

title: Questions One to Three
lead: Rubric as printed: Attempt QUESTION ONE and any three (3) questions, in 3 hours. Question One is compulsory and carries 17½ marks, as does every other question. Each question below appears three times over: the examiner's words, a reading of them, then the answer.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
a. Briefly explain the following with symbolic examples:

   (i)  Super type
   (ii) Specialisation
   (iii)Total specialisation
   (iv) Disjoint rule                                        (4 mks)

blocks.label: Break it down
blocks.working:
Given four EER terms; Figure 1, the EMPLOYEE2 relation with EmpID and CourseTitle underlined as a composite key; and a three-relation schema (BRANCH, STAFF, PROPERTYFORRENT).

Asked to explain with symbolic examples (not merely define, so each term needs a worked instance); to show all possible determinants and name the type of each dependency; and to write six SQL queries.

Marks 4 + 2½ + 11 = 17½. The SQL is worth nearly two thirds of a compulsory question, so it is the part to practise, not the definitions.

Taught Module Two Unit 2 (EER terms), Module Four Unit 1 (determinants), Module Five Unit 2 (SQL).

Trap in (b) the marks are only 2½, yet "show ALL possible determinants" means both EmpID alone and the composite. Naming one earns half. In (c)(vi) "no staff assigned" is an anti-join: NOT IN or a LEFT JOIN with IS NULL, never a plain join.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.working:
(a) EER terms, with symbolic examples. Super type: a generic entity type holding the attributes common to its subtypes, for example EMPLOYEE over HOURLY and SALARIED. Specialisation: the top-down process of defining subtypes of a supertype (EMPLOYEE specialised into HOURLY and SALARIED). Total specialisation: every supertype instance must belong to at least one subtype, drawn as a double line. Disjoint rule: an instance may belong to at most one subtype, drawn as a circle marked d. (Module Two, Unit 2.)

(b) Determinants in EMPLOYEE2. A determinant is the attribute, or set of attributes, on the left of a functional dependency. In EMPLOYEE2(EmpID, CourseTitle, Name, DeptName, Salary, DateCompleted):

EmpID determines Name, DeptName and Salary: a partial dependency, since EmpID is only part of the key. The composite (EmpID, CourseTitle) determines DateCompleted: a full functional dependency. Because a partial dependency exists, the relation is in 1NF but not 2NF.

(c) The six SQL queries. Solved at length in Module Five, Unit 2.4.

(i)   SELECT * FROM STAFF WHERE salary > 100000 ORDER BY salary DESC;
(ii)  SELECT branch_no, COUNT(*) FROM STAFF GROUP BY branch_no;
(iii) SELECT branch_no, AVG(salary) FROM STAFF GROUP BY branch_no;
(iv)  SELECT * FROM PROPERTYFORRENT WHERE rooms > 3 AND rent > 80000;
(v)   SELECT p.property_no, p.type, p.rent, s.fName, s.lName
      FROM PROPERTYFORRENT p JOIN STAFF s ON p.staff_no = s.staff_no;
(vi)  SELECT branch_no FROM BRANCH
      WHERE branch_no NOT IN (SELECT branch_no FROM STAFF);

The amounts are written 100000 and 80000 in SQL because the Naira sign and the thousands commas are presentation, not data; say so in one line under your answer and you have shown you read the question rather than ignored the currency.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: a. Explain two (2) limitations of the file-based approach to data processing.   (2 mks)

blocks.label: Break it down
blocks.working:
Given nothing but definitions for (a) to (c); for (d), Figure 2, a crow's-foot EER for a University Dining Service with five entity types.

Asked to explain, then to transform a diagram into relational schemas. "Transform" means produce the relations, not describe how you would.

Marks 2 + 2 + 5½ + 8 = 17½. Part (d) alone is worth more than (a), (b) and (c) together, and it is the only part that cannot be bluffed.

Taught Module One Units 2.1 to 2.5 (file-based limits, DBMS, abstraction); Module Three Unit 2.4 (the transform).

Trap the multivalued attributes in Figure 2 are printed in braces, {Ingredient} and {Skill}. Each becomes its OWN relation, not a column. Miss that and the transform loses several marks even though the rest is right.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.working:
(a) Two limitations of the file-based approach. Data redundancy and inconsistency, since the same fact is stored and updated in several files; and program-data dependence, since a file's structure is coded into every program that reads it. (Module One, Unit 2.1.)

(b) A DBMS. The software that lets users define, create, maintain and control access to a database, for example MySQL or Oracle. (Module One, Unit 2.2.)

(c) Data abstraction, three levels. Hiding storage detail so each user sees only what they need: the external level (per-user views), the conceptual level (all tables and relationships), and the internal level (physical storage). (Module One, Unit 2.5.)

(d) The University Dining transform. Worked in full at Module Three, Unit 2.4. Each multivalued attribute becomes its own relation, and each many-to-many becomes a link relation:

MENU(menuID, menuDescription, menuType)          PK menuID
DISH(dishID, dishName, prepTime)                 PK dishID
DISH_INGREDIENT(dishID, ingredient)              PK (dishID, ingredient)
MENU_DISH(menuID, dishID)                        PK (menuID, dishID)
EVENT(eventID, eventDate, eventLocation, eventTime)   PK eventID
MENU_EVENT(menuID, eventID)                      PK (menuID, eventID)
STAFF(empID, name, salary, supervisorID)         PK empID  FK supervisorID -> STAFF
STAFF_SKILL(empID, skill)                        PK (empID, skill)
WORK_SCHEDULE(empID, eventID, startTime, endTime, position)
   PK (empID, eventID)

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
a. (i)    Would you choose a database system instead of simply storing data in operating
          system files? Justify your answer with two points.        (5 marks)
   (ii)   When would it make sense not to use a database system?    (2.5 marks)

blocks.label: Break it down
blocks.working:
Given a judgement call in (a), and in (b) a narrative description of a law firm.

Asked (a) asks "Would you choose ... Justify with two points", so an unjustified yes scores nothing; (a)(ii) asks when it would make sense not to, the word printed in italics because it inverts the question. (b) asks you to draw.

Marks 5 + 2.5 + 10 = 17½. The diagram is worth ten, so budget accordingly.

Taught Module One Units 2.1 and 2.7; Module Two Unit 2 (EER).

Trap the same person or organisation may be a plaintiff in one case and a defendant in another. That is two many-to-many relationships between the same pair of entity types, not one. Drawing a single "involved in" line is the error the question is built to catch.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.working:
(a) Database or operating-system files. (i) Choose a database: it gives one shared, consistent copy with concurrency control, and enforces integrity, security and data independence centrally, none of which loose files provide. (ii) It would not be worth it for a small, single-user, single-application task with little data and a fixed structure, where a full DBMS is pure overhead. (Module One, Units 2.1 and 2.7.)

(b) EER for the law firm. Each CASE (caseNumber, dateOpened, dateClosed, judgmentDescription) is brought by one or more plaintiffs and is against one or more defendants. A plaintiff or defendant is a LEGAL ENTITY (entityNumber, name, netWorth), which is either a PERSON or an ORGANISATION. Because the same entity can be plaintiff in some cases and defendant in others, draw two many-to-many relationships between LEGAL ENTITY and CASE. requestedJudgment is a property of the plaintiff relationship, not of the entity, so it sits on that relationship.

title: Questions Four to Six
lead:
The remaining three, any two of which you would answer alongside Question
  One. Full working, with the module named where a topic is treated at length.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: a. Describe the relational Data model.                       (2 ½ mks)

blocks.label: Break it down
blocks.working:
Given five relation schemas: Emp, Dept, D_Loc, Project and Works_on.

Asked to describe, to explain six operations with examples (six, and each needs an example), and to write the relation algebra, meaning expressions in symbols, not English and not SQL.

Marks 2½ + 6 + 9 = 17½. Six operations for six marks is one mark each with an example; do not write an essay on selection and run out of time.

Taught Module Three Unit 1 (the model); Module Five Unit 1 (algebra, all eight operations and their symbols).

Trap (iii) says "work on all the projects controlled by" a department. "All" is the signature of division (÷). A join and a count will not do it and is the commonest wrong answer.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.working:
(a) The relational data model. It represents all data as relations, that is two-dimensional tables of rows and columns, with relationships between them expressed by shared values rather than by pointers, and it is manipulated by relational algebra. (Module Three, Unit 1.)

(b) Six operations, with examples. Selection (σ, choose rows: σrent<500(PROPERTY)); projection (π, choose columns: πfName,lName(STAFF)); union (∪, all rows of either); set difference (−, rows of one not in the other); Cartesian product (×, every pairing); and join (⋈, a product kept only where a condition holds). (Module Five, Unit 1.1.)

(c) The three algebra expressions. Worked at Module Five, Unit 1.4.

(i)   HQ     ← σ DName='Headquarters' (Dept)
      Result ← π Fname, Lname ( Emp ⋈ Dno=DNum HQ )

(ii)  Abuja  ← σ P_Loc='Abuja' (Project)
      Result ← π PNo, DNo, Mgr_SSN ( Abuja ⋈ DNo=DNum Dept )

(iii) A314   ← π PNo ( σ DNo='A314' (Project) )
      Result ← π Fname, Lname ( ( π ESSN,PNo (Works_on) ÷ A314 ) ⋈ ESSN=SSN Emp )

In (ii) the manager's name needs one more join, Dept to Emp on Mgr_SSN = SSN, if the examiner wants the name rather than the SSN. Say which you read it as. In (iii) the division is what "all the projects" demands.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
a. Given the following database concept in (I-III), answer question (i-ii):
      I.   The data definition language.
      II.  The data manipulation language.
      III. The data model.
      (i)  Which of the following enumerations (I) to (III) plays an important role in representing
           information about the real world in a database?          (½ mk)
      (ii) Explain each concept briefly; your explanation should reflect the answer for your
           choice.                                                  (6 mks)

blocks.label: Break it down
blocks.working:
Given three enumerated concepts (DDL, DML, data model); and a long narrative about a technology company's offerings.

Asked to choose then explain; and to develop an EER model using the crowfoot notation. The notation is specified, so a Chen diagram scores badly however correct.

Marks ½ + 6 + 11 = 17½. The model is worth eleven, nearly two thirds.

Taught Module One Unit 2.3 and Module Three Unit 1 (DDL/DML); Module Two Unit 2.6 (this exact EER, worked).

Trap read the completeness constraints out of the words. "Offerings are of two separate types" is total and disjoint; but "There are repair, maintenance, and other types of services" makes SERVICE only partial. And "some products never require repair" plus "many potential repair services for a product" fixes the optionality and the cardinality of that relationship.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.working:
(a) The choice and the three concepts. (i) The data model. (ii) A data model is the set of concepts (entities, relationships, attributes and constraints) used to describe the structure and meaning of data, so it is the one that represents information about the real world. The data definition language defines that structure to the DBMS (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), and the data manipulation language operates on the data held in it (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). Neither language models reality; they realise and query a model. (Module One, Unit 2.3.)

(b) Crow's-foot EER for the technology company. Worked in full at Module Two, Unit 2.6. OFFERING (offeringID, description) is total and disjoint over PRODUCT (productName, standardPrice, dateOfFirstRelease) and SERVICE (unitName, conditionsOfService). SERVICE is partial and disjoint over REPAIR (cost) and MAINTENANCE (hourlyRate), because the paper allows "other types of services". A REPAIR repairs a PRODUCT: optional on the product side (some products never require repair), many on the repair side (many potential repair services for a product). CUSTOMER (customerID, name, address, phoneNumber) purchases OFFERING, an optional many-to-many carrying purchaseDate and contactPerson; and a SERVICE performed is billed to a CUSTOMER, carrying datePerformed, dateDue and amountDue, which is a separate relationship from the purchase because a customer may be billed for a service they did not purchase.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
a. Explain the following relational terms briefly:                  (3 mks)
      (i)   Schema
      (ii)  Alternate key
      (iii) Tuple

blocks.label: Break it down
blocks.working:
Given three relational terms; and StaffPropertyInspection with four data rows, six named functional dependencies and the primary key stated as (propertyNo, iDate).

Asked to draw the FD diagram, to briefly explain transitive dependency (so two or three sentences, not a page), and to normalise to 3NF with all actions well stated and the output tables presented with their primary keys identified. The Note is itself worth marks.

Marks 3 + 2½ + 2 + 10 = 17½. The normalisation is ten, and the Note tells you those ten are for the working, not just the final tables.

Taught Module Three Unit 1 (the terms); Module Four Unit 1.4, where this exact relation is normalised step by step.

Trap the key is given, so do not spend time deriving it. Work 1NF to 2NF to 3NF in named steps and show the relation you split off at each one; a correct final answer with no working cannot score ten.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.working:
(a) The three terms. Schema: the structure of a relation, its name together with its attributes, for example STAFF(staffNo, fName, lName, branchNo). Alternate key: a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key. Tuple: one row of a relation, one complete record. (Module Three, Unit 1.)

(b)(i) and (iii) are worked step by step at Module Four, Unit 1.4. Taking the attribute as sName throughout, and the key as (propertyNo, iDate):

(ii) Transitive dependency. A non-key attribute depends on the key only through another non-key attribute. Here staffNo → sName: sName is determined by staffNo, and staffNo is itself determined by the key, so sName reaches the key only via staffNo. That is what 3NF removes, by moving sName into a relation of its own keyed on staffNo.

The 3NF result:

Property(propertyNo, pAddress)                   PK propertyNo
Staff(staffNo, sName)                            PK staffNo
PropertyInspection(propertyNo, iDate, iTime, comments, staffNo, carReg)
   PK (propertyNo, iDate)   FK propertyNo -> Property, FK staffNo -> Staff

Steps to state: 1NF, the table already holds single values, so it qualifies once the repeating property address is understood as belonging to the property. 2NF, remove the partial dependency fd2 (propertyNo → pAddress) into Property. 3NF, remove the transitive dependency fd3 (staffNo → sName) into Staff. carReg is left on the inspection because fd4 makes it depend on staffNo together with iDate, which is not a determinant available in either split relation.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: How to spend the three hours
blocks.html:
Question One is compulsory and mixes EER terms, a functional-dependency reading and SQL, so it rewards broad preparation. For your three chosen questions, pick the ones whose long parts you are surest of: the transforms (Q2d, Q5b), the algebra (Q4c) and the normalisation (Q6b) each carry the most marks and are the most mechanical once learned. Draw every diagram large and label every cardinality; an unlabelled line scores little.

Watch the mark text as you triage. This paper does not write marks the same way twice: most parts read "mks", Question Three alone reads "marks" and prints 2.5 as a decimal, and Question Six drops to the singular "mk". None of that changes what a part is worth, but a candidate skimming for the big numbers can misread 2.5 as 25.
